concept_definition: In sports, a fixture is a match or game scheduled to take place on a particular date.
A match in sports is a contest in which two players or teams compete against each other.
A tournament is an organized series of sports contests in which participants compete to determine a winner.
A sports competition in which teams or players compete to determine who is the best.
In sports, a final is the last match or contest in a competition, which decides the winner.
In a sports competition, a semifinal is one of the two matches that decide which competitors advance to the final.
A round in a sports tournament in which eight competitors or teams play matches, usually to decide which four advance to the semifinals.
A part of a sports competition in which teams or players are divided into groups and play matches within their groups to decide who advances to the next stage.
In sports, an upset is a win by a team or player expected to be weaker than the opponent.
In sports, a draw is a match that ends with both sides having the same score.
In sports, an equal score between competitors or teams, so neither side is ahead; a tie may be the final result of a game or match.
A tiebreak is a method or extra period of play used in sports to decide the winner when the score is level.
In sports, a kickoff is a kick that starts or restarts a match or period of play.
In sports, overtime is extra playing time added when the score is tied at the end of regular time, to determine the winner or continue the game.
In sports, a timeout is a short break in play requested by a team.
In sports, an action by a player that breaks the rules of the game.
In sports, a save is a goalkeeper's successful stop of a shot that would otherwise enter the goal.
In sports, an act in which a team loses possession of the ball to the opposing team.
In sports, an equalizer is a goal that makes the scores of the competing teams level.
In sports, a hat trick is when one player scores three goals or points in a single game.
In sports such as tennis, a set is a unit of a match made up of a group of games or points.
In sports, a match point is a point that, if won by a player or team, ends the match in their favor.
In sports, singles is a match in which one player competes against one other player.
A sports match in which two pairs of players compete against each other.
In sports, a heat is one of several preliminary races or contests in which competitors try to qualify for a later round.
A relay is a race in which team members take turns completing parts of the course, usually passing an object such as a baton between them.
In sports, a false start is starting a race or play before the official signal or permitted time.
In sports, a photo finish is a race finish so close that a photograph or finish-line camera is needed to determine which competitor crossed first.
In sports, doping is the illegal use of drugs or other banned substances to improve an athlete’s performance.
A turn is the period in a board or table game when one player may make a move or take an action.
In chess, a check is an attack on the opponent's king that must be escaped, blocked, or stopped.
In chess, checkmate is a position in which a player's king is under attack and cannot escape capture, ending the game.
In chess, a short form of checkmate: a position in which a player's king is under attack and has no legal move to escape.
In chess, a stalemate is a position in which the player to move has no legal move and their king is not in check, so the game ends in a draw.
In chess, a special move in which the king moves two squares toward a rook, and that rook moves to the square the king crossed.
In chess, promotion is the rule that lets a pawn reaching the last rank become a queen, rook, bishop, or knight.
In chess, the endgame is the final stage of a game, when most pieces have been exchanged and relatively few remain on the board.
In chess, a pin is a situation in which a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it to attack.
In chess, a discovered check occurs when a piece moves out of the way and reveals an attack by another piece on the opposing king.
In chess, a perpetual check is a repeated series of checks that prevents the opponent from escaping or winning, usually leading to a draw.
In chess, a draw claim or draw condition that occurs when the same position, with the same player to move and the same possible moves, appears three times during a game.
In chess, a position in which a player is forced to make a move, but every legal move worsens their position.
In chess, a blunder is a very bad move that seriously worsens a player's position or can lead to losing.
In basketball, a free throw is an unopposed shot taken from the free-throw line, awarded after certain fouls.
In basketball, a three-pointer is a successful shot taken from beyond the three-point arc, worth three points.
In basketball, a jump ball is when an official tosses the ball upward between two opposing players, who jump to try to tap it to a teammate and begin play.
In basketball, a tip-off is the jump ball used to start a game.
In basketball, a rebound is gaining possession of the ball after a shot misses the basket.
In basketball, to take possession of the ball from an opponent by legally intercepting a pass or taking the ball from them.
In basketball, a violation in which a player holding the ball moves their feet illegally without dribbling.
In basketball, a violation that occurs when a player dribbles, stops, and then dribbles again, or dribbles with both hands at the same time.
In basketball, a shot made just before the game clock expires, with the ball reaching the basket before the buzzer sounds.
In basketball, an air ball is a missed shot that touches neither the rim nor the backboard.

concept_definition: In basketball, a swish is a successful shot that passes through the hoop without touching the rim or backboard.
In basketball, a personal foul is illegal physical contact by a player against an opponent.
In basketball, a technical foul is a penalty called for unsporting behavior or a rule violation that does not involve illegal physical contact.
In basketball, a double-double is a performance in which a player records at least 10 in two statistical categories, such as points and rebounds, in one game.
In basketball, a triple-double is a game in which a player reaches at least 10 in three statistical categories, such as points, rebounds, and assists.
In tennis, deuce is a score of 40–40, when a player must win two consecutive points to win the game.
In tennis, advantage is the position a player gains by winning the point immediately after deuce, leaving them one point from winning the game.
In tennis, a fault is a serve that fails to land in the correct service box.
In tennis, a double fault occurs when a player fails to serve the ball legally on both attempts, losing the point.
In tennis, a foot fault is a serving fault called when the server steps on or over the baseline before hitting the ball.
In tennis, a let is a serve that touches the net but lands in the correct service court, so the server must serve again.
In tennis, a break point is a point on which the receiver can win the game and break the server’s serve.
In tennis, an unforced error is a mistake a player makes on a shot they could reasonably have returned or played successfully without exceptional pressure from the opponent.
A period in a baseball game in which each team has a turn batting until three of its players are put out.
In baseball, a strike is a pitch counted against the batter, usually because it passes through the strike zone without being hit or the batter swings and misses.
In baseball, a ball is a pitch that is outside the strike zone and that the batter does not swing at.
In baseball, a strikeout is an out recorded when a batter receives three strikes.
In baseball, a walk is when a batter reaches first base after the pitcher throws four balls.
In baseball, a single is a hit on which the batter reaches first base safely without advancing on an error or a fielder’s choice.
In baseball, a double is a hit that lets the batter reach second base safely.
In baseball, a triple is a hit on which the batter reaches third base without being put out.
In baseball, a hit that lets the batter circle all the bases and score, usually without being put out.
In baseball, a home run hit when runners occupy all three bases, scoring four runs.
In baseball, a run is a point scored when a runner legally reaches home plate.
In baseball, a run batted in (RBI) is credited to a batter when their plate appearance results in a runner scoring, subject to scoring rules.
In baseball, an out is a recorded dismissal that removes a batter or runner from active play for that half-inning.

In baseball, a stolen base is a base a runner safely advances to while the pitcher is delivering the ball, without the advance being credited to a hit, a putout, an error, a force play, or a wild pitch or passed ball.
In baseball, a double play is a continuous play in which the defense records two outs.
In baseball, a batted ball that rises high into the air and is usually caught before it touches the ground.
In baseball, a batted ball that lands outside the foul lines is a foul ball.
In baseball, an error is a misplay by a fielder that allows a batter or runner to reach a base or advance when they otherwise would not have.
In baseball, a no-hitter is a game in which one team’s pitcher or pitchers allow the opposing team no hits.
In cricket, an innings is one team's turn to bat, ending when its allotted overs are completed or its batting side is dismissed.
In cricket, an over is a set of six legal deliveries bowled by one bowler from one end of the pitch.
In cricket, a maiden is an over in which the bowler concedes no runs from the bat or other scoring, excluding any penalty runs.
In cricket, a boundary is a hit that reaches or crosses the edge of the playing field, scoring four runs if the ball first touches the ground or six if it does not.
In cricket, a century is an innings in which one batter scores 100 or more runs.
In cricket, a half-century is an innings in which one batter scores 50 runs.
In cricket, a duck is a batter's score of zero in an innings.

In cricket, leg before wicket (LBW) is a way a batter can be dismissed when the ball hits the batter’s body instead of the bat and would otherwise have hit the stumps, subject to the laws’ conditions.
In cricket, a run out is a dismissal that occurs when a batter’s wicket is broken by the ball while the batter is out of their ground and attempting to run.
In cricket, a no-ball is an illegal delivery called by the umpire, for which the batting team is awarded an extra run and the ball usually remains in play.
In cricket, a wide is a delivery judged too far from the batter to be hit, which counts as an extra and is not one of the over's legal deliveries.
In cricket, a bye is a run scored by the batting team when a delivered ball passes the batter without touching the bat or body and the batters run.
In cricket, a run scored when the ball deflects off the batter’s body or clothing (but not the bat) and the batters run, provided the ball was not a no-ball.
In cricket, an option for the team batting first to make the other team bat again immediately after its first innings, when the other team has scored sufficiently fewer runs.
In cricket, a hat trick is when one bowler takes a wicket with each of three consecutive deliveries.
In cricket, an appeal is a fielder’s request to the umpire to give the batter out.
In cricket, an international match between national teams played over up to five days, in which each team can bat twice.
In American football, a scoring play in which a player carries the ball into or catches it in the opponent’s end zone, worth six points.
A kick in American football that sends the ball through the opponents’ goalposts and is worth three points.
A kick attempted after a touchdown in American football that is worth one point if successful.
A scoring play in American football in which a team, immediately after scoring a touchdown, runs or passes the ball into the opponent’s end zone to earn two extra points.
A two-point score in American football awarded when a player tackles an opponent who has the ball in the opponent’s own end zone.
In American football, the act of a center passing the ball backward between the legs to a teammate to start a play.
In American football, one of a team's four attempts to advance the ball at least ten yards and earn a new set of attempts.
In American football, a new set of four downs awarded to the offense after it gains the required yards, usually ten.
A tackle of the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage before he can throw a forward pass.
In American football, an act in which a player who has possession of the ball loses control of it before being downed or scoring.

In American football, a catch of a punt or kickoff made after the receiver signals for a fair catch, allowing the receiver to catch the ball without being tackled and requiring the play to end immediately.
A penalty in American football for illegally grabbing or restraining an opponent who does not have the ball.
An interception returned by the defender for a touchdown in American football.
In American football, a change to the called play made by the quarterback at the line of scrimmage before the snap.
In checkers, a move in which a piece makes two captures in succession during the same turn.
An ice hockey restart in which an official drops the puck between two opposing players, who try to gain possession.
A violation in ice hockey in which a player shoots the puck from their own half of the rink across the opposing team’s goal line without it being touched, subject to rule-specific exceptions.
A situation in ice hockey in which a team has more players on the ice because an opponent is serving a penalty.
A situation in ice hockey in which a team with one or more players serving penalties defends against the opposing team’s power play.
The act of using a hockey stick held in both hands to forcefully hit or push an opponent with the shaft while it is off the ice.
In ice hockey, an infraction in which a player carries, swings, or contacts the puck or an opponent with a stick held above the permitted height.
A penalty in ice hockey for using a stick, leg, or other part of the body to cause an opponent to fall.
A penalty in ice hockey for violently pushing or checking an opponent into the boards.
In ice hockey, a tiebreaking contest in which players take turns making one-on-one shots against the opposing goalie to decide a tied game.
In golf, a score of one stroke under par on a hole.
A golf score of two strokes under par on a hole.
A golf score of three strokes under par on a hole.
In golf, a score of one stroke over par on a hole.
In golf, a score of two strokes over par on a hole.
A golf shot in which a player gets the ball into the hole with the first stroke on that hole.
An attempt in golf to strike the ball with a club, whether or not the ball is hit; it counts as one stroke under the rules.
An unofficial second shot allowed in golf after a poor first shot, usually without counting the first shot on the scorecard.
A golf format in which players or teams compete to win individual holes, with the winner determined by the number of holes won rather than the total number of strokes.
A golf format in which each player or team counts the total number of strokes taken to complete the round, and the lowest total wins.
In go, a position in which a stone or group has only one liberty and can be captured on the opponent’s next move.
A repeating capture pattern in go in which a player may not immediately recapture the same stone and recreate the previous board position.
In Go, the status of a group as either able to remain on the board permanently or certain to be captured.
A position in go in which opposing groups share liberties and neither player can capture the other without putting their own group in danger.
In go, the initiative that lets a player make a move requiring a response, so they can play elsewhere next.
A standard sequence of moves in a local area of a Go board that is considered balanced for both players.
A rugby score awarded when a player grounds the ball in the opponent’s in-goal area, worth five points.
In rugby, a kick at goal awarded after a try, which can score additional points if successful.
A scoring try awarded by the referee in rugby when an opponent commits an offence that would probably have prevented the try from being scored.
A score in rugby made by kicking the ball through the goalposts immediately after it has bounced off the ground from a drop kick.
A rugby set piece in which the forwards from each team bind together and push against each other to contest possession of the ball.
A rugby restart in which the ball is thrown in between two lines of players who try to catch or tap it.
In rugby, a contest in which players from both teams, on their feet and in physical contact, push over the ball on the ground.
A phase of play in rugby in which a ball carrier remains on their feet while players from both teams bind together and push around them to contest possession.
The contest for possession of the ball at a ruck or near a tackled player in rugby.
In rugby, an infringement that occurs when a player loses the ball or knocks it forward and it touches the ground or another player before being regained.
An illegal pass in rugby in which a player throws or passes the ball forward toward the opponents’ goal line.
A temporary suspension in rugby that requires a player to leave the field and prevents them from taking part for ten minutes.
A contest in which two boxers fight under boxing rules.
A three-minute period of a boxing bout, separated from the next period by a rest interval.
A boxing hold in which a fighter holds the opponent to stop them from punching.
A boxing result in which a boxer ends the bout by knocking the opponent unconscious or unable to continue.
A boxing stoppage in which the referee ends the bout because a boxer cannot safely continue, even though the boxer has not been counted out after a knockdown.
In boxing, an event in which a boxer is knocked to the floor by a punch and must take a count from the referee.
In boxing, the referee’s spoken count to ten over a knocked-down boxer, who must rise before the count ends to avoid losing by knockout.
A boxing victory on points in which the judges disagree about which boxer won.
An official event before a boxing bout at which the boxers are weighed to confirm they meet the required weight limits.
In a card game, a set of cards played one by one by the players in a round, usually won by the player who plays the highest-ranking card according to the rules.
An offer in a card game to win a specified number of tricks, often with a named trump suit or no trump.
A contract in a trick-taking card game, especially bridge, in which no suit is designated as trump.
In a card game such as bridge, the final bid that sets the goal the declarer must make.
A match in a card game, especially bridge, that is won by the first side to win two games.
In a card game, a bid or contract to win all thirteen tricks in a deal.
In a trick-taking card game such as bridge, a bid or contract to win twelve of the thirteen tricks.
In a card game with bidding, a trick won by a side beyond the number of tricks it contracted to take.
In contract bridge, a trick that the declaring side fails to take below the number of tricks required by its contract.
A short track-and-field running race run at maximum speed.
An athletics race in which runners sprint over a series of barriers called hurdles.
A long-distance running race in athletics that covers 42.195 kilometers.
An athletics road race covering 21.0975 kilometers (13.1 miles), half the distance of a marathon.
A running race held over natural, open terrain rather than on a standard track.

An athletics event in which competitors walk as fast as possible while maintaining continuous contact with the ground and keeping the supporting leg straight from first contact until it passes beneath the body.
A track-and-field competition in which athletes perform a jumping or throwing discipline, rather than a running race.
An athletics event in which competitors run up to and jump over a horizontal bar without knocking it down, aiming to clear it at the greatest height.
An athletics event in which competitors run along a runway and jump as far as possible into a sand pit.
An athletics jumping event in which an athlete runs up and performs a hop, a step, and a jump into a sand pit, aiming to achieve the greatest distance.
An athletics event in which competitors use a long flexible pole to propel themselves over a high crossbar.
An athletics event in which competitors throw a heavy metal ball, called a shot, as far as possible from a circle.
A track-and-field throwing event in which an athlete spins and throws a heavy metal ball attached to a wire and handle as far as possible.
An athletics competition in which each athlete competes in ten track-and-field events, usually over two days, and receives a combined score.
An athletics competition in which each athlete competes in seven track-and-field events, with performances scored to determine the overall winner.
A swimming race in which competitors may use any stroke, though they usually use front crawl.
A swimming race in which competitors use all four strokes—backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly, and freestyle—in a set order.
A single day's race or leg in a multi-day bicycle race.
A bicycle race held over several days in which each day's racing is a separate stage and the overall winner is determined by the combined results.
A bicycle race in which riders start separately and compete to complete a course in the fastest time.
A short time trial held at the start of a stage race to determine the opening standings or starting order.
In a stage race, the overall ranking of riders by their cumulative time across all stages, with the lowest total time leading.
A bicycle race held on a short closed circuit, usually with many laps and a winner determined by the finish or points.
A track cycling race in which riders follow a motorized pacer before sprinting for the finish.
A track cycling event in which riders compete in several different races, with points awarded across the races to determine the overall winner.
A track cycling race in which riders start on opposite sides of the track and try to catch one another or record the fastest time over the set distance.
A track cycling race in which teams of two riders take turns racing, usually by exchanging with a hand sling.
A volleyball attack that lands in the opponent’s court or otherwise cannot be returned, winning the point outright.
The movement of volleyball players one position clockwise around the court after their team wins the right to serve.
A volleyball rally won by the receiving team, giving it the right to serve.
A poker hand containing two cards of one rank, two cards of another rank, and one unrelated card.
A poker hand containing three cards of the same rank.
A poker hand consisting of five cards in consecutive rank order, regardless of suit.
A poker hand consisting of five cards of the same suit, not in consecutive rank.
A poker hand containing three cards of one rank and two cards of another rank.
A poker hand containing four cards of the same rank.
A poker hand of five cards in consecutive rank, all of the same suit.
In poker, a hand consisting of the ace, king, queen, jack, and ten of the same suit.
A poker hand that contains no pair or other combination and is ranked by its highest card.
The best possible poker hand given the cards available at that moment.
A small forced bet that each player puts into the pot before the cards are dealt in poker.
A forced poker bet that a player must make before the cards are dealt.
In poker, a bet in which a player wagers all the chips they have in play.
The stage of a poker hand when the remaining players reveal their cards to determine the winner.
A poker loss in which a hand that was a strong favorite to win is defeated by an opponent who catches unlikely cards.
A skiing or snowboarding race in which competitors descend a course by zigzagging between closely spaced gates.
A skiing or snowboarding race in which competitors descend a course marked by widely spaced gates, making broad turns as quickly as possible.
A timed alpine skiing race in which competitors ski a fast course of widely spaced gates, combining speed with more turns than a downhill race.
An alpine skiing or snowboarding race in which competitors descend a long course as fast as possible.
A skiing event in which competitors descend a ramp, launch into the air, and are scored for the distance and style of their jump.
A skiing or snowboarding competition in which athletes perform tricks from one large jump and are judged on their attempts.
A skating event or discipline in which a man and a woman skate together as a team.
A figure-skating competition segment in which skaters perform a set of required elements within a time limit, before the free skate.
In figure skating, a program in which a skater performs a set of required elements and other chosen movements, usually as the second segment of a competition.
A gymnastics event in which a gymnast performs a choreographed routine of tumbling and other skills on a spring floor.
A gymnastics competition in which a gymnast's scores from every event are combined to determine the overall result.
A gymnast’s complete performance on one apparatus, made up of a sequence of skills performed under the rules of gymnastics.
A score in judo and some other martial arts awarded for a decisive throw, pin, or submission that wins the contest.
A hold in martial arts or wrestling that forces an opponent to give up.
A wrestling victory in which a competitor holds an opponent's shoulders against the mat so they cannot escape.
A win in wrestling or martial arts awarded when a competitor pins the opponent according to the rules.
A backgammon win in which the loser has not borne off any checkers.
A situation in association football in which an attacker is in an offside position when a teammate plays the ball and then becomes involved in active play.

A restart in association football awarded when the ball crosses the goal line after last touching a defending player, allowing the attacking team to kick it from the corner arc nearest where it went out.
A set piece in association football awarded to the attacking team when the ball crosses the goal line after last touching a defender, taken from the corner arc nearest where it went out.
A restart in association football awarded to a team after an opponent commits a foul, allowing the team to kick the ball without interference from opponents until it is in play.
A direct shot taken from the penalty spot in association football, with only the goalkeeper allowed to defend against it.
A series of kicks from the penalty mark used to decide an association football match that remains drawn after extra time.
A restart in association football in which the defending team kicks the ball from its goal area after the attacking team last touched it before it crossed the goal line without a goal being scored.
A method of restarting play in association football in which a player throws the ball onto the field from behind the touchline after it has gone out of play.
The two additional periods played in an association football knockout match when the score is tied after regular time, to determine a winner.
In association football, a match in which a team concedes no goals.
A goal in association football that a player accidentally scores against their own team.
A caution shown by the referee to a player in association football for misconduct, which is recorded and may lead to a sending-off if the player receives another.
A card shown by the referee in association football to dismiss a player from the match.
A formal caution given to a player by the referee in an association football match and recorded in the match report.
An offense in association football in which a player illegally touches the ball with a hand or arm.
A match in association football between teams from the same city or region that are local rivals.
